title: Why a marketing site should be fast before it is clever
metaTitle: A fast marketing website, before the clever
excerpt: A fast marketing website earns the right to be clever. Paint the page quickly, then add the one motion that explains something. Slow decoration reads as carelessness.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it. The quiet desk fits a piece about making the page fast before adding cleverness.
caption: Speed is a property of the page, measured before the decoration is praised. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should be fast on a marketing site?
faqs.answer: The first view of the page: the headline, the offer, and the way to talk to you. Google's Core Web Vitals describe a good load as the largest content appearing within 2.5 seconds. If that moment is late because a decorative animation has to start first, the cleverness is in the way.

faqs.question: Is animation always a problem?
faqs.answer: No. One motion that shows a relationship or a change can help. Looping decoration that delays the text, shifts the layout, or runs for its own sake does not. Ship the fast page, then add the motion you can justify in a sentence.

faqs.question: How should a founder ask for speed?
faqs.answer: Ask which page is the largest content, what happens when someone taps the main button, and whether anything jumps after load. Ask for those checks on a phone. A promise that the site will feel premium is not a substitute for the check.

markdown:
A fast marketing website is one where the offer is visible and usable before any cleverness starts. The headline, the proof, and the way to talk to you should show up as the page. Motion, custom cursors, and entrance sequences are optional. They are allowed after the page is already quick, and only when they explain something.

Cleverness on a slow page reads as carelessness. A visitor does not experience your taste first. They experience the wait. If the wait is long, the animation that finally plays feels like the reason they waited. That is a bad trade for a company that is asking to be trusted with a project.

## What fast means in public numbers

Google's Web Vitals initiative names three Core Web Vitals for loading, interactivity, and visual stability. [web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) states the good thresholds plainly. Largest Contentful Paint should occur within 2.5 seconds of when the page starts loading. Interaction to Next Paint should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift should stay at 0.1 or less. Those are the targets for a good experience, judged at the 75th percentile of page loads, on mobile and on desktop.

You do not need to memorize the acronyms to use them. Ask three questions. When does the main headline or image actually appear? When someone taps the primary button, how long before the page responds? Does anything jump after they started reading? A founder can watch those three on a phone and know whether the clever layer is affordable.

A marketing page often fails the first question because the largest thing is an image or a webfont that arrives late, or because nothing is allowed to appear until an intro animation finishes. It fails the second when a heavy script has to wake up before a menu or a form will answer. It fails the third when a banner, a cookie bar, or a late font pushes the headline down after the person has already aimed a finger.

## Cleverness that waits its turn

Decide the first paint as if motion did not exist. Type, color, the sentence, the action. That version should be complete. If you turned the display off halfway through a load, a person should still be able to read the offer. Hanabi's standard on the marketing site is the same idea: static where it can be, images that do not block the words, and motion that is not required to understand the page.

Then add the one motion that explains something. A panel that shows where it came from. A state that changes, so a person sees that a choice registered. A short transition between two views that would otherwise feel like a jump cut. One is usually enough. A page with five simultaneous ideas of cleverness has no hierarchy, and the main idea loses.

Looping decoration is the usual culprit. A background that never settles, a cursor that lags behind the pointer, a hero that replays every time you scroll back. These fight reading. They also tend to be the code that costs the first paint. If you cannot say what the motion explains, remove it and measure again.

## How slow cleverness gets built

It gets built when the reference is another site's highlight reel, watched on a fast connection, on a laptop, by someone who already intended to be impressed. The reel hides the load. Your visitor is on a phone, on the way to a decision, and they have not agreed to watch a film.

It also gets built when motion is specified before the content. A storyboard of entrances assumes the headline will be short, the image will be light, and the font will be instant. Then the real headline wraps, the photograph is several times larger than the layout needs, and the font blocks the text. The animation is faithful to the storyboard and late to the person.

Write the performance budget into the same note as the visual idea. The largest image has a maximum size. The webfont has a fallback that is allowed to show. Scripts for animation do not run ahead of the headline. These are design constraints. They are not a cleanup task for the week after launch.

## What to ask for in a build

Ask to see the page on a phone, on a throttled connection, before you judge the motion. If the team only ever demos on the office network, you are reviewing a different product from the one customers get.

Ask which element is the largest content, and whether it is the element you actually want people to see first. A giant background video can become the largest paint while the headline waits. That is a choice, and it is usually the wrong one for a company site.

Ask for a still version. The page with motion reduced, or with motion removed, should still be the page. If the still version looks broken, the design depended on movement to make sense. Fix the design. People who prefer less motion, and people whose browsers are simply busy, will live in that version.

Hanabi builds with Next.js, React, and TypeScript, and the marketing pages stay static where they can. The stack is not the argument. A slow page can be built in any stack. The argument is the order of work: the readable page first, the single useful motion second.

## A simple order for the team

1. Ship the words, the action, and the images at the size they need.
2. Measure the three questions on a phone.
3. Add one motion, and only if you can say what it explains.
4. Measure again. If the page got worse, the motion does not stay.

That order feels less exciting than starting with the animation. It is how a marketing site stays something you are willing to send to a buyer. Taste that arrives late is not the taste they will remember. The wait is.

The three measures deserve their own plain-language explanation, with an example of each. [Core Web Vitals in plain language](/blog/core-web-vitals-in-plain-language) is that piece, if you want the names and the thresholds without a performance glossary.

When you want a company site that is fast and then, where it helps, precise, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The craft standard is clarity, including the decision to leave cleverness out when it costs the first view.
